html:
William Perry traced the way many university students gradually rethink what "knowledge" is and how they ground their own judgments. He saw movement not as the accumulation of facts but as a restructuring of epistemology, passing through nine "positions" that cluster into four broad phases.

Stages

At first, in Dualism (Positions 1 & 2), the world is starkly black-or-white. Truths are handed down by infallible authorities-professors, textbooks, religious figures-and the learner’s task is to memorize and reproduce them accurately. When disagreements among authorities surface, the novice treats them as temporary errors: someone must be right, someone wrong; uncertainty merely signals that the correct answer hasn’t yet been located.

As exposure widens, the student discovers that experts often disagree in ways not immediately resolvable. This ushers in Early Multiplicity (Position 3): multiple right answers seem to coexist, yet they are still judged as "not-yet-verified" truths rather than valid perspectives. By Late Multiplicity (Position 4) the learner concedes that some questions may never have one correct answer and begins to defend the legitimacy of opinions-"everyone’s entitled to their view." Here, intellectual effort can feel pointless, so motivation often shifts to pragmatics: do what the professor likes, play the game, get the grade.

A turning point comes when the student grasps that evidence and reasoning can weigh competing claims. Enter Contextual Relativism (Positions 5 & 6). Knowledge is recognized as contextual: good answers are "better" because they are supported by coherent argument, fit available data, or serve agreed-upon aims. Evaluation becomes a disciplined craft, and the learner’s own voice grows more assured, now grounded in method rather than authority or opinion.

Finally, in Commitment within Relativism (Positions 7 - 9), the individual accepts that choices must be made despite ambiguity. One articulates personal commitments-to a career path, ethical code, or research stance-while remaining aware that new evidence could demand revision. Responsibility shifts inward: the self becomes author and steward of its beliefs, values, and actions. Instead of seeking certainty, the learner nurtures a living dialogue between conviction and doubt, continuously re-examining assumptions in light of experience and argument.

Perry emphasized that progression is neither automatic nor linear; students may linger, loop, or compartmentalize different domains at different levels. What propels movement are challenges that make existing epistemic habits insufficient-diverse peers, open-ended problems, professors who model inquiry rather than dictate answers-and a supportive climate that rewards reflection over rote compliance. The reward is a mind capable of both critical analysis and purposeful commitment, comfortable navigating complexity without surrendering to either dogmatism or apathetic relativism.
